messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 53
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: Oceania
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Airline Pilot
- Trauma Type: Torture
- Pcl5: 70

He is 53, a commercial airline pilot from Oceania, and when he first begins talking about what happened, he does it the way he says he learned to survive it: carefully, with control, and only in short bursts. For years he has made a career out of remaining calm in enclosed spaces, monitoring instruments, anticipating danger before others notice it. He says that before the trauma, this kind of vigilance felt like competence. Now it follows him everywhere.

Several years earlier, while traveling overseas on a layover between flights, he is detained by security forces after being mistaken for someone else. At first he believes the confusion will be sorted out quickly. He shows identification, explains that he is an airline pilot, repeats the name of his hotel and his employer. Instead, he is taken to a windowless room and held there. The first night stretches into something shapeless. Questions are shouted in a language he only partly understands. When his answers do not satisfy them, he is struck, restrained, deprived of sleep, and made to stand for long periods until his legs shake. Over the following days, the men who interrogate him alternate between mock friendliness and cruelty. They hood him, threaten his family, pour water over him until he panics that he is drowning, and leave him alone in darkness long enough that time loses meaning. He becomes preoccupied with tiny details—the scrape of a chair leg, the smell of damp fabric, the sound of keys—because details are the only things he can hold onto while he waits for the door to open again.

He is eventually released without explanation. By then he is dehydrated, bruised, and profoundly disoriented. He remembers getting home more as fragments than as a complete sequence: airport lights that feel too bright, his wife’s face collapsing when she sees him, the humiliation of not being able to reassure her. In the first weeks after returning, he sleeps in brief, jagged intervals. He startles awake convinced he cannot breathe. In dreams he is back in the cell, unable to tell whether his eyes are open or closed. Sometimes he wakes swinging his arms, once striking the bedside lamp hard enough to shatter it. He apologizes over and over to his wife, but he can see that she has started sleeping lightly, listening for changes in his breathing.

He returns to flying sooner than he now thinks he should have. He tells himself that routine will help, that the cockpit is a place where procedures make sense and training overrules panic. Outwardly, he remains capable. He passes checks, speaks evenly over the radio, and runs through preflight lists with the same precision as always. But inside, his world has narrowed. A closed cockpit door suddenly feels different from what it used to. During one flight, when a jump seat rider knocks unexpectedly, the sharp rap of knuckles sends a jolt through him so intense that for a moment he loses track of the checklist item in front of him. He recovers quickly, but afterward sits in his car in the parking lot with both hands gripping the steering wheel, ashamed of how frightened he has been.

At home he becomes harder to reach. His wife says he is present in the room but not really with her. He avoids crowded restaurants, avoids news from the region where he was detained, avoids conversations that begin with, “What was it like over there?” He tells people he is tired from work. He begins inspecting locks repeatedly before bed, then tells himself this is sensible, not excessive. If someone approaches him from behind, his body reacts before his mind catches up. He can feel his heart pounding in his throat, his shoulders tightening, his fists clenching. He hates this automatic violence in himself. He has grandchildren now, and when one of them throws a wet towel over his head during a game, he shouts so fiercely that the child bursts into tears. The look on his daughter’s face stays with him for weeks.

He says the worst part is not the fear but the constant sense of contamination, as if the men who tortured him still dictate the terms of his life. He used to love layovers in unfamiliar cities; now he researches every destination obsessively, scans hotel exits, and sleeps with a chair wedged under the door handle. He cannot tolerate being restrained even casually. During a routine medical procedure when a nurse asks him to hold still, sweat runs down his back and he has to fight the urge to tear the equipment off and leave. He knows these reactions are irrational in the present moment, and that knowledge does not diminish them.

His wife has heard more of the story in fragments than in full. He worries that if he tells it straight through, he will somehow bring the cell into the house. Yet the story is already there—in the dark circles under his eyes, in the way he maps every room he enters, in the silence that falls over him when he hears keys jangling in a corridor. He still flies, still dresses with care, still speaks in the composed, measured tone of a senior pilot. But he moves through the world as though danger has become the hidden weather system underneath ordinary life, always present, always waiting to break.
